summary:
MARS-1 is a browser game where students command a crewed outpost on Mars or the Moon and must keep it alive for a mission they choose (5 to 60 sols). Every sol they balance the same trade-offs NASA flight directors face: power (solar output degraded by dust, RTG backup), life support (O2, water and food per astronaut, recycling efficiency like the ISS), radiation shielding (regolith and water against solar storms) and food production in a greenhouse. Random emergencies always offer three options with real costs, and every failure ends with a technical 'autopsy' that explains the science behind it.

What makes it different is that real NASA data enters the game: the solar storm on Sol 3 is compared with the strongest flare of the last 30 days from NASA DONKI, solar energy is compared with NASA POWER measurements, and historical missions (Opportunity's 2018 dust storm, Apollo 13) can be replayed in the order events really happened. A teacher can give the class a mission code so everyone plays the same mission and compares decisions. It runs offline with saved copies if the internet fails, which matters for schools in Bolivia. The goal: make engineering trade-offs tangible and fun for young students, not oversimplified or overwhelming.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

MARS-1 puts the student in the role of commander of a crewed outpost on Mars or the Moon. The player picks the scenario, the mission length (5 to 60 sols), a strategic directive (Survival, Production or Full Shield) and then, sol by sol, decides how to spend limited power, credits and crew time: repair panels, expand the greenhouse, thicken regolith shielding, upgrade the ECLSS, run research in the lab. Supplies follow the mission length (initial cargo and a cargo ship every 15 sols). Random events (dust storms, solar particle events, equipment failures, discoveries) always offer three options with real costs and risks. Winning shows a score and the lessons learned; losing shows a technical 'autopsy' with what went wrong and what to do next time. A career history keeps each commander's profile.

HOW IT WORKS

A pure simulation engine (TypeScript, tested with Vitest) computes each sol from real engineering relations: power balance with solar efficiency degraded by electrostatic dust on Mars and long shadow periods on the Moon, plus RTG backup; metabolic consumption per astronaut (0.84 kg O2, 2.5 L water, 0.62 kg food per sol); regenerative life support with the Sabatier reaction and water electrolysis and 85-98% recycling (ISS standard); greenhouse photosynthesis with LED PAR spectra; and radiation dose from galactic cosmic rays and solar particle events attenuated by hydrogen-rich materials (water and regolith), following NASA-STD-3001 limits.

REAL NASA DATA IN THE GAME

- On Sol 3 a solar storm arrives; the game asks NASA DONKI for the strongest solar flare of the last 30 days and compares it with the emergency (an X12 flare, like the one that reached Mars on 20 May 2024).

- NASA POWER provides the solar energy that actually reached the ground in Santa Cruz de la Sierra, Bolivia, in recent weeks, compared with the ~43% that reaches Mars.

- Historical missions: Opportunity and the 2018 dust storm, and Apollo 13 (1970), with events in the order they happened.

- Real images from the NASA Image and Video Library (PIA22329, PIA22521, PIA26302) with credits.

- Every request has an 8-second limit; if it fails the game uses a saved copy and labels it 'SAVED COPY', so it works in classrooms with poor connectivity.

FOR THE CLASSROOM

A teacher shares a mission code and the whole class plays the same mission, with the same events in the same order, so students can compare decisions and discuss trade-offs. A STEM Learning Center inside the game explains each concept with real cases (ISS, Curiosity, InSight, Perseverance, Artemis) and a glossary.

IMPACT

Space STEM content is often either oversimplified or too complex for young students. MARS-1 makes the trade-offs tangible: students feel that more shielding means less power for food, that skipping a repair today costs a crew member tomorrow. It is free, runs in any browser, needs no installation, and is in Spanish, aimed at students in Bolivia and Latin America.

TOOLS

React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Lucide icons, Web Audio API (procedural sound, no audio files), localStorage (auto-save), Vitest, GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages. AI assistants (Claude) were used for brainstorming, research, coding, debugging and writing; the team designed the game, decided the mechanics and reviewed the science.

CREATIVITY AND DESIGN CHOICES

We chose a commander's console look with live telemetry, alarms and a 'black box' history chart so it feels like mission control. Every event has three options, never one obvious answer, because real missions are about trade-offs. We also wanted today's real Sun to matter in the game, so the danger is not just invented.
